steps.say: Every student remembers Meckel through the rule of twos, and the rule earns its place. Two percent of children carry the remnant, two feet from the valve, two inches long, with two kinds of ectopic tissue, usually presenting around two years. Gastric mucosa leads the ectopic list at sixty percent with pancreatic tissue far behind at five. Recite the rule and the diagnosis rarely escapes you.
steps.tx: The **rule of 2s in Meckel diverticulum** packs the whole disease into one mnemonic. It affects **2%** of children, sits within **2 feet** of the ileocecal valve, measures **2 inches** long, holds **2 types** of ectopic tissue with **gastric** mucosa at **60%** and pancreatic tissue at **5%**, and presents around **2 years** of age. A painless massive bleed in a toddler should trigger the rule instantly.

steps.say: A toddler who passes a large bloody stool without any pain points straight at Meckel. Acid from the ectopic gastric patch ulcerates the neighbouring ileal wall, which has no defence against it. The blood looks brick red or maroon and the child stays comfortable, a combination that separates Meckel from fissures and colitis. Volume can be startling, so resuscitate while you investigate.
steps.tx: **Painless massive rectal bleeding** is the signature of a bleeding Meckel diverticulum. Ectopic **gastric acid** ulcerates adjacent unprotected ileal mucosa, producing sudden **brick-red or maroon** stools while the child stays comfortable and playful. Pain would point toward fissure or colitis instead, so the painless massive bleed in a toddler means Meckel until the scan says otherwise.

edges: no fissure, no pain, no diarrhoea

steps.say: The Meckel scan hunts ectopic stomach, not the diverticulum itself. Technetium 99m pertechnetate is snatched up by gastric parietal cells wherever they sit, lighting the ectopic patch on camera. Cimetidine and glucagon sharpen the picture by holding tracer in the patch and quieting bowel motion. A positive blush in the right lower quadrant in a bleeding toddler is diagnostic.
steps.tx: The **technetium-99m pertechnetate scan** lights up ectopic stomach wherever it hides. **99mTc-pertechnetate** is taken up selectively by gastric **parietal cells**, so the ectopic patch glows on scintigraphy. Sensitivity climbs with **cimetidine** pretreatment plus **glucagon**, which trap tracer and still bowel motion. A focal right lower quadrant blush in a bleeding toddler confirms the diverticulum.

steps.say: Juvenile polyps are the commonest cause of painless rectal bleeding in a well child. More than eighty percent of childhood gut polyps are solitary hamartomas hanging in the rectosigmoid on a stalk. The child strains, passes bright blood over formed stool, and is otherwise thriving. One polyp snared at colonoscopy usually ends the story completely.
steps.tx: **Juvenile polyps characteristics** reassure more often than they alarm. These hamartomas form over **80%** of childhood gut polyps, typically solitary, **pedunculated**, and seated in the **rectosigmoid**. Bleeding is painless **haematochezia** over formed stool in a thriving child, and single polypectomy at colonoscopy cures most cases without any surveillance burden.

points: Five or more polyps, or any plus family history
right.title: When to suspect a syndrome

steps.say: Count polyps and ask about family before dismissing recurrent juvenile polyps. Juvenile polyposis syndrome is autosomal dominant through SMAD4 or BMPR1A, defined by five or more colorectal polyps, polyps throughout the tract, or any juvenile polyp with a family history. These children carry real cancer risk and enter colonoscopic surveillance. The gene result schedules the whole family, not just the child.
steps.tx: **Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome** turns a benign polyp into a family diagnosis. This autosomal dominant condition from **SMAD4** or **BMPR1A** mutations is defined by at least **5** juvenile polyps in the colorectum, polyps scattered through the gut, or any juvenile polyp with a **family history**. Affected children need scheduled surveillance, and cascade testing pulls in parents and siblings.

vis.alt: Endoscopic view of a pedunculated juvenile polyp beside histology showing cystic glands and inflamed stroma.
vis.caption: Juvenile polyp with cystic glands and inflamed stroma seen at endoscopy and under the microscope. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Dark freckles around the mouth plus a blocked small bowel spell Peutz-Jeghers. The STK11 gene, also called LKB1, litters the gut with hamartomas while painting melanin spots on lips and digits. Polyps here intussuscept rather than bleed, so the child arrives with colicky pain and vomiting. Surveillance spans gut, breast, and gonads because cancers strike beyond the bowel.
steps.tx: **Peutz-Jeghers syndrome** pairs unmistakable skin signs with small bowel polyps. **STK11** (LKB1) mutation produces mucocutaneous **melanin pigmentation** around the mouth and digits plus hamartomatous small bowel **polyps** that intussuscept. Presentation is colicky obstruction more than bleeding, and lifelong surveillance must cover intestinal, breast, and gonadal cancers.

rows: Dark spots on lips and digits

steps.say: Hundreds of adenomas in a teenager mean APC until proven otherwise. Familial adenomatous polyposis carpets the colon with adenomatous polyps carrying certain cancer risk without surgery. Screening sigmoidoscopy starts at ten to twelve years, and prophylactic colectomy follows in late adolescence. Extracolonic clues such as CHRPE, osteomas, and desmoids should prompt the gene test earlier.
steps.tx: **Familial Adenomatous Polyposis** converts teenage polyps into a surgical timetable. **APC** mutation grows hundreds to thousands of **adenomatous polyps** with **100%** colorectal cancer risk, so screening **sigmoidoscopy** starts at age **10-12** and prophylactic **colectomy** lands in late adolescence. Extracolonic flags like CHRPE, osteomas, and desmoid tumours should trigger testing before the colon fills.

vis.alt: Panel of familial adenomatous polyposis findings: carpeted colorectal polyps, duodenal and gastric polyps, an adenoma histology field, CHRPE, an osteoma, and a desmoid.
vis.caption: Familial adenomatous polyposis: colorectal carpet, duodenal adenomas, CHRPE, osteoma, and desmoid. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A big head plus genital freckling plus mixed polyps points to PTEN. Cowden and Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndromes share germline PTEN mutations with macrocephaly, lipomas, and penile freckling alongside hamartomatous gut polyps. Measure the head, examine the skin, and send the gene test when the pattern fits. Surveillance here is broader than the bowel, covering thyroid and breast from early on.
steps.tx: **PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome** links head size, skin, and gut. **Cowden** and **Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba** syndromes carry germline **PTEN** mutations with **macrocephaly**, lipomas, **penile freckling**, and mixed gastrointestinal polyposis. The head circumference and skin exam make the diagnosis before the scope does, and surveillance extends to thyroid and breast alongside the bowel.
